n: In this session we will learn to determine ethanol by gas-liquid chromatography, that is, GLC. The plan is as follows: toxicology of ethanol, the theory and design of gas chromatography, preparation, sample, measurement, calculation and control. The aim is the qualitative and quantitative determination of alcohols in blood and urine by GLC. Key terms: injector, column, thermostat, detector, retention time, alkyl nitrite and internal standard. The working order is as follows: preparation, calibration, sample, measurement, calculation and cleaning.

t: Why ethanol is determined by GLC
n: Why is ethanol determined specifically by GLC? By its pharmacological action, ethyl alcohol belongs to the group of narcotic substances. When drunk, it passes quickly into the blood; after 5 minutes it can be detected in the blood. In the liver it is rapidly oxidised, 90-99 % to CO2, which is why the analysis is carried out quickly. According to the figures in the book, the boiling point of ethanol is 77-78.5 °C.

t: Ethanol in the body: the pathway
n: What path does ethanol take in the body? Ethanol that is drunk passes quickly into the blood and is oxidised in the liver. Oxidation produces CO2 and water, which accounts for 90-99 %. The rest is excreted through breath and the kidneys. In poisoning, the concentration of alcohol in urine is considerably greater than in blood. The stomach, liver, kidney and brain may be taken for analysis.

t: History of chromatography: Tswett, Martin and Synge, James
n: Now the history of chromatography. The method of chromatography was first applied in 1903 by M. S. Tswett to separate a complex mixture obtained from green plants. Then Martin and Synge proposed paper chromatography and received the Nobel Prize; they showed that a gas can be used as the mobile phase. In 1952 James and Martin developed the methods of gas-adsorption and gas-liquid chromatography.

What GLC is; we will look at two groups. Gas chromatography is divided into gas-adsorption and gas-liquid chromatography, that is, GLC. In the gas-adsorption method, the stationary phase is a porous solid. In the gas-liquid method, the stationary phase is a liquid coated on a porous solid. In both methods the mobile phase is a gas. The difference lies only in the stationary phase.

Let us list the parts of a gas chromatograph. The parts: gas source, reducer, injector, chromatographic column, thermostat, detector and recording device. The gas from the source, that is, the cylinder, nitrogen or argon, having passed through the reducer, is fed into the column together with the sample. The column is placed in the thermostat. The quantity of gas is measured in special rheometers. At the outlet the detector registers the signal, and the recording device records it.

t: Parts of the GC and their functions: analytical parts
n: The analytical parts of the GC and their functions. The injector is the device for introducing the sample. In the chromatographic column the process of separating the substances takes place. The thermostat heats the chamber in which the columns are placed to the required temperature. The detector, converting the change in the properties of the gas stream into an electrical signal, identifies the components. The recorder writes down the results of the analysis.

t: Parts of the GC and their functions: gas supply
n: Now the parts of the gas supply. The cylinder is intended to supply the chromatograph with the mobile phase, that is, the gas. The flow stabiliser ensures that the gas stream is supplied evenly. The manometer measures the gas pressure entering and leaving the column. The flow meter measures the quantity of gas leaving the instrument.

Let us consider the essence of separation. First the mixture is introduced into the heated gas stream; the liquid turns into gas in the thermostat at high temperature. In the column the substances undergo adsorption and desorption many times between the stationary and the gas phases. The efficiency of separation depends on the distribution coefficient of the substances. At the end, the detector records the change in the composition of the emerging gas.

On the distribution coefficient K. GLC is the redistribution and separation of substances between a gas and a liquid. Separation is explained by the distribution coefficient: K equals C stationary divided by C mobile. The sample in the gas stream is in the vapour state, is then absorbed in the stationary liquid phase and is redistributed according to K. If K is small, the substance is little absorbed in the stationary phase and leaves the column quickly.

Open information on Kristallyuks and Chromatec. The catalogue of the Kristallyuks-4000M lists flame-ionisation, that is, FID, and electron-capture, that is, ECD, detectors, as well as packed and capillary columns. The thermostat operates from room temperature, +4, to 270 °C; the programming rate is 0.1-120 °C/min. The sensitivity of the FID is given in the catalogue as 2×10⁻¹² g C/s. In the Chromatec Kristall 5000 series, up to 4 detectors and 3 vaporisers are fitted in one instrument; this is information from the vendor's catalogue.

On the column. Columns are U-shaped, spiral or ring-shaped. The internal diameter is from 2 mm to 12-15 mm, the length 2-20 m. Columns are made mainly of glass, copper, brass or steel. For the qualitative determination of alcohols, the column size is 100 × 0.6 cm.

Now the stationary phase and the solid support. INZIM brick-600 is taken as the solid support, particle size 0.25-0.5 mm; it was treated with sodium hydroxide and sodium alkyl sulphates, 0.3 g each. The stationary phase is Shostakovsky's balsam, that is, vinylin, impregnated in a ratio of 1:5 to the solid phase. The mobile phase, that is, the gas, is nitrogen.

t: Carrier gas, sorbent and factors of separation
n: Carrier gas, sorbent and factors of separation. The main inert gases: nitrogen, helium, argon. Sorbents: silica gel, aluminium oxide, activated carbon, synthetic porous substances, chemosorb and polysorb. Separation depends on uniform density of packing of the column with sorbent, the nature of the sorbent, the gas velocity and the constancy of temperature. In the gas-adsorption method the stationary phase is a solid sorbent: activated carbon, silica gel, aluminium oxide.

Let us look at the classification of detectors. Detectors are divided into integral and differential types. The signal of an integral detector is proportional to the total mass of the substance in the gas stream; the line is stepped. Differential detectors show the change in the quantity of substance per unit time; they are divided into concentration and flow types. The katharometer belongs to the concentration type, and the flame-ionisation detector to the flow type. By design there are also the electron-capture and thermionic detectors.

We compare the katharometer, FID and ECD detectors. In the analysis of most volatile medicinal substances, the katharometer is used, based on the change in thermal conductivity of gases. The katharometer is universal and simple, but its sensitivity is lower than that of flame-ionisation detectors, 10⁻²-10⁻³. The flame-ionisation detector is a flow detector and is based on ionisation in a hydrogen flame; the conductivity of the flame changes. Electron-capture detectors are considered the most sensitive.

t: Katharometer and FID: principle of operation
n: How do the katharometer and FID work? The katharometer detects the change in thermal conductivity of gases: the resistance of a heated conductor changes accordingly. It is a concentration detector, universal, with a sensitivity of 10⁻²-10⁻³, that is, low, but simple. In the flame-ionisation detector, an organic substance burns in a hydrogen flame between two electrodes, forming ionised radicals. The electrical conductivity of the flame changes depending on the concentration of the substance burned. Electron-capture detectors are the most sensitive.

The chromatogram and retention time. The curve on the chromatographic paper is called a chromatogram; each peak is characteristic of a separated substance. Retention time is the time that elapses from introducing the substance into the column until its maximum emergence, that is, the distance. If conditions are kept the same, retention time is a parameter determining the quality of the substance, that is, it shows which substance it is. The height of the peak, in turn, indicates how much alcohol there is, that is, the quantity.

t: Chromatogram: peak, dead time and true time
n: The peak, dead time and true time on a chromatogram. The straight line on the chromatogram indicates the passage of the pure mobile phase, and the peak indicates that a substance has emerged. The chromatogram is characterised by parameters such as retention time, height, base and area. The true retention time equals the retention time of the substance minus the dead retention time, that is, tm: t true equals t total minus t m. The height of the peak depends on the quantity of alcohol.

The first preparation: tightness of the injector. Before work, make sure that the septa in the injector block are tightly closed. Soap solution is applied with the syringe needle to the place where the substance is introduced; if no bubble forms, the injector is tightly closed. If a bubble forms, the rubber septum is replaced in the presence of the teacher. The check is repeated throughout the session.

The second preparation: the microsyringe. The check is carried out with 1 µl syringes: 0.5 µl of acetone is drawn into the syringe. The acetone is dropped onto filter paper; a microdrop forms at the tip of the needle, and a small wet spot remains on the paper. If no microdrop forms, the microsyringe is recalibrated by turning the screw that holds the needle.

The third preparation: sensitivity. Air is introduced into the chromatograph; when the maximum of the curve equals half the height, the sensitivity level is quickly switched to the "100" position. The height of the water curve then decreases. The analysis of water vapour and air is checked at the beginning, middle and end of the session.

Analysis conditions. The temperature of the column and detector block is 75 °C. The carrier gas is nitrogen, at a rate of 50-60 ml/min; detector current 60-100 mA. Recording scale 1:1; the chart-paper tape speed is 720 mm/h.

t: Alcohol and methane: comparison of conditions
n: We compare the conditions of the analysis of alcohol and methane. In alcohol analysis, a GC with a katharometer is used: column 100 × 0.6 cm, 75 °C, nitrogen 50-60 ml/min. In methane analysis, a Svet-110 chromatograph, a polysorb-1 column, 50 °C, vaporiser 150 °C, nitrogen 30 ml/min. For methane the detector is flame-ionisation; retention time 3 minutes. In the table the methane column is given as 100 mm × 3 mm.

The reaction converting alcohols to alkyl nitrites. A mixture of alcohols is converted to alkyl nitrites with trichloroacetic acid and sodium nitrite. Reagents: mixture of alcohols 0.5 ml, 50 % trichloroacetic acid 0.5 ml and 30 % NaNO2 0.25 ml. The reaction is carried out in a penicillin vial under a rubber stopper, shaken for 1 minute. The product is alkyl nitrites in the gas phase; 2 ml of the gas phase is introduced into the injector.

Preparing the standard mixture. 0.5 ml of the mixture of alcohols is placed in a penicillin vial containing 0.5 ml of 50 % acid. The vial is closed with a rubber stopper, fitted into a special clamping device and mixed. 0.25 ml of 30 % sodium nitrite is introduced with a syringe; it is mixed for 1 minute, and 2 ml of the gas-air portion is taken. Then it is introduced into the injector, and the time and peaks are noted.

t: Preparing a blood and urine sample
n: Preparing a blood and urine sample. 0.5 ml of 50 % trichloroacetic acid is placed in a penicillin vial, and 0.5 ml of blood or urine on top. The vial is closed with a rubber stopper, fitted into the fixator and the substances are mixed thoroughly. 0.25 ml of 30 % sodium nitrite is introduced with a 1 ml syringe. It is shaken for 1 minute; with a 5 ml syringe, 3 ml is taken from the air-gas portion inside the vial.

Injecting the sample and recording the time. The air-gas mixture is injected quickly into the injector block, and the recording of the chromatogram is observed. A stopwatch is started with the injection; the time to the height of each curve is noted. The time obtained is compared with the time obtained from the standard solutions.

Calibration and internal standard. The student must draw up an accurate calibration table with the selected internal standards. First the internal standard is selected, then the standards are converted to alkyl nitrites. The alcohols are accurately taken from the gas phase and injected into the injector, and a chromatogram is obtained. From this the calibration table is drawn up. Determining relative retention parameters and selecting an internal standard are among the review questions.

Methods of quantitative determination. In GC analysis, the quantity of a substance is determined in three ways: internal standard, absolute calibration and internal normalisation. The quantity of alcohol is determined by the internal standard method, with propyl alcohol taken as the internal standard. Absolute calibration and internal normalisation are only listed in the book. The accuracy of the method is quite high: the relative error is around ±1.0-1.5 %.

Internal standard and calibration graph. Alkyl nitrites are several times more volatile than the corresponding alcohols; therefore the alcohols are converted to alkyl nitrites. Propyl alcohol is taken as the internal standard; the calculation is performed from a calibration graph. The graph is constructed from the ratio of the peak height of ethyl nitrite, h1, to the peak height of propyl nitrite, h2, and the concentration of the substance. An exact volume is taken from the vapour-gas phase and injected into the chromatograph.

The advantages and disadvantage of GLC. GLC is a universal method; the column separates complex mixtures into individual components. Little time and a small quantity of substance are used in the analysis; the sensitivity is sufficient. The accuracy of the method is high: the relative error is around ±1.0-1.5 %. The disadvantage is that some liquid stationary phases are volatile and unstable.

Criteria for identification and repetition. Substances are distinguished by the curves on the chromatogram; the retention time, that is, the distance, is calculated and the height is measured. For qualitative analysis the retention time must coincide with the standard. For quantitative analysis, the peak height and the calibration table are used. The height of the curve depends on the quantity of alcohols. The examination of the alkyl nitrites is repeated three times and entered in special tables.

Methods of qualitative, that is, identity, analysis. The first is identification by retention parameters. The second is comparison with a standard substance or a mixture of them. The third is carrying out chemical reactions before and after chromatographic analysis. The fourth is combining GLC with physical methods such as UV, IR, mass spectrometry, luminescence and NMR.

Let us establish what the book contains on calculation. The book gives the peak time and height, the internal standard and calibration table, and a threefold repetition. The book contains no exact calculation formula, no instrument buttons or menu, and no limit of detection, that is, LOD. Therefore we do not add a formula of our own here. If a doubtful result is obtained, the check is repeated together with the teacher.

Safety and quality control. The tightness of the injector septa is checked with soap solution and monitored throughout the session. If a bubble forms, the rubber septum is replaced in the presence of the teacher; with a doubtful result, the check is carried out together with the teacher. The microsyringe is checked before work with 0.5 µl of acetone. The analysis of water vapour and air is checked at the beginning, middle and end of the session; the alkyl nitrite check is repeated three times and entered in the table.
On the status of the instrument manual. In the catalogue card of the Kristallyuks-4000M, no operating manual is indicated.

t: Case: the smell of fusel oil
n: Case: the smell of fusel oil. In students who drank a weak alcoholic drink, nausea, abdominal pain, dizziness and drowsiness were observed. A smell of fusel oil came from the breath of the poisoned. Task: to isolate a volatile toxic substance from the internal organs of a body and to show the procedure of chemical-toxicological analysis.

t: Forensic chemical conclusion: drawing up the report
n: The forensic chemical conclusion and drawing up the report. The report of the examination consists of three parts: introduction, description, that is, the descriptive part, and conclusion. The introduction states the basis, the performer, the object and the aim. In the description, the appearance of the object, its pH medium, consistency and the chemical methods of examination are written in detail, without abbreviations. In the conclusion, the toxic substances detected and not detected on the basis of the examination are stated by name. The report is certified by the expert's signature and the time of writing; abbreviating words and putting conventional signs is forbidden.

To conclude. In GLC substances are separated in the column and registered in the detector; quality is determined by retention time, and quantity by height. Review questions include the sections of the chromatograph, the significance of the detector, the reducer, the chromatogram and the retention period. Questions are also asked on the resorption and elimination of ethyl alcohol and on the advantages of GLC over other methods. Repeat the working order: preparation, calibration, sample, measurement, calculation and cleaning.

Questions for review. What sections does a chromatograph have, and in which section is the mixture separated? What is the significance of the detector? What are the types of detectors and how do they work; what is a chromatogram and by what parameters is it characterised? What is the retention period of a substance in the column? Give the concept of the separation coefficient of substances. How are relative retention parameters determined and an internal standard selected? What are resorption and elimination of ethyl alcohol; what are the advantages of GLC over other methods?
